area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why full power with approach trim makes the nose rise sharply and swing left, demonstrate the elevator trim stall from the right seat at a safe altitude while you narrate it, recover and retrim, and teach a learner to keep control of every go-around.
why: The elevator trim stall shows what can happen when a pilot applies full power for a go-around without keeping positive control of the airplane [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Many stall/spin accidents happen during go-arounds, and a nose-high trim setting is named as a causal factor [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. Only flight instructor applicants may be tested on it [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], so your demonstration may be the only safe look your learners ever get.

prereading.what: The elevator trim stall: objective, where it happens, the entry, the recovery and retrim, and the 18 common stall errors.
prereading.label: AFH 5-20 to 5-21

prereading.what: Go-arounds: power, attitude and configuration, the low-airspeed trim setting, rough trim, flap retraction and the go-around errors.
prereading.label: AFH 9-11 to 9-12

prereading.what: Longitudinal stability: downwash on the tail, why speed and power change the pitch, and the thrust line.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-16 to 5-17

prereading.what: Trim systems: how the elevator trim tab moves the elevator, and retrimming after power, attitude or configuration changes.
prereading.label: PHAK 6-10 to 6-11

prereading.what: The stall recovery template, including nose-down trim, and the stall training altitude.
prereading.label: AFH 5-15 to 5-16

prereading.what: The CFI stall training plan: the elevator trim effect in slow flight and the elevator trim stall demonstration.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C 200

prereading.what: Supervising practice, taking control from an anxious learner, and distractions while changing configuration or trim.
prereading.label: AIH 9-8 to 9-9

warmup: Think first: your learner is on short final, full flaps, trimmed for the approach, when the tower says go around. They push the throttle in all at once and their hands go light on the yoke. The nose climbs past anything you have seen in a normal climb and the airplane swings left. Which two things made the nose come up, and why did it go left? What will you say in the next two seconds, and what do you want their hands and feet doing? Then ask yourself: how would you show this to them at 5,000 ft so it never surprises them at 200 ft?

key_terms.def: A stall that can follow full power for a go-around with the airplane trimmed nose-up for the approach glide, when the pilot does not keep positive control [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
A small hinged surface on the trailing edge of the elevator, set from the flight deck, that holds the elevator where the pilot wants it so constant pressure is not needed [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].
Trim tab moved down, so the airflow forces the elevator trailing edge up, the tail down and the nose up [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].
A first, quick trim adjustment after setting the climb attitude, to relieve adverse control pressures; finer trim follows once things settle [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Air driven back by the propeller. In this stall, more propwash over the tail adds to the trim and makes the nose rise sharply [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
The spiral of the slipstream that strikes the vertical fin and yaws the airplane; strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
At a high AOA the downward-moving blade takes a bigger bite, moving the center of thrust right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Air deflected down by the wing that pushes down on the horizontal stabilizer; less downwash at low speed or low power means less tail-down force [[1:113|PHAK 5-16]] [[1:114|PHAK 5-17]].
Discontinuing a landing; done by power, attitude and configuration, in that order [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
The power applied for the go-around in this demonstration (CFI ACS AI.X.G.S5); applied smoothly, without hesitation [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
The maximum speed with the flaps extended, the top of the white arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]; set by the air loads on the flaps [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].
The belief that the approach will surely end in a safe landing; one of the two common reasons a go-around is delayed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

body.p: The elevator trim stall demonstration shows what can happen when the pilot applies full power for a go-around without maintaining positive control of the airplane [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. It is a demonstration-only maneuver that only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform on a practical test, but every pilot should know the situations that cause it, recognize it developing and act to prevent it [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

The AFH says the demonstration teaches four habits: smooth power applications, overcoming strong trim forces, keeping positive control to hold safe attitudes, and proper and timely trim. It also builds the ability to avoid the actions that cause it, recognize it approaching and act before a full stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The point of it all is to never have an elevator trim stall during an actual go-around [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Why your learners need it: AC 61-67C says many stall/spin accidents in the takeoff and climbout phases happen during go-arounds, and names as a causal factor the pilot's failure to keep positive control because of a nose-high trim setting or premature flap retraction [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. The CFI ACS says the flight instructor normally demonstrates Tasks F, G and H to learners for familiarization and stall/spin awareness, and that private and commercial certification does not include them (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X).

This lesson assumes the general stall material from Power-Off Stalls (AI.X.C) and Power-On Stalls (AI.X.D): critical AOA, stall cues, the recovery template and the four left-turning forces. Here we add only what is special to this stall: the trim, the strong pitch-up and left turn when power comes in, the forward pressure and retrim, and why it bites on go-arounds.

callout.text: Skill element AI.X.G.S9 reads: "Describe and demonstrate conditions that lead to an elevator trim stall for future avoidance." The words are graded, not only the flying. Plan them.

check.q: Name the four habits the AFH says this demonstration builds.
check.a: Smooth power applications, overcoming strong trim forces, keeping positive control to hold safe attitudes, and proper and timely trim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

chunks.title: What nose-up trim is doing on final

body.p: Trim systems relieve the pilot of holding constant pressure on the controls. The most common setup in small airplanes is a single trim tab on the trailing edge of the elevator, worked by a wheel or crank with a position indicator [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

The tab moves opposite to the elevator. With the trim set full nose-up, the tab moves full down; the air under the tail pushes on it and forces the elevator trailing edge up, so the tail goes down and the nose goes up [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

Why so much nose-up trim on final? Most airplanes are built nose heavy and balanced by a downward force on the tail. Part of that force comes from the wing's downwash hitting the stabilizer, and the slower the airplane flies, the less downwash and the less tail-down force, so the nose tends to drop [[1:113|PHAK 5-16]]. Closing the throttle also reduces the downwash, and the nose pitches down [[1:114|PHAK 5-17]].

Application: a slow, power-off glide therefore needs a lot of back pressure, and a good pilot trims it all away. By short final the trim is far nose-up. The design rules expect this: the trimming device must be able to hold the airplane in a normal glide with the power off [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

The normal trim technique is to set power, pitch attitude and configuration first, then trim off the remaining pressure; as power, attitude or configuration change, retrimming is needed [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]. A go-around changes all three at once, so the old trim is now badly wrong.

callout.text: Application: in the glide, have the learner look at the trim indicator and then let go of the yoke for a moment. 'The trim is holding the nose up for us now. Remember that when the power comes in.' Note that a zero mark on the trim indicator is not necessarily neutral trim [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

check.q: Your learner rolls in full nose-up trim. Which way does the elevator trim tab move, and what does that do to the elevator?
check.a: The tab moves down; the airflow under the tail forces the elevator trailing edge up, so the tail goes down and the nose up [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

chunks.title: Why full power makes the nose rise and swing left

body.p: The AFH puts it in one line: the combined effects of more propwash over the tail and the elevator trim make the nose rise sharply and turn to the left, and with the throttle fully advanced the pitch attitude goes above the normal climbing attitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The airplane does this by itself. Nobody is pulling.

The PHAK explains the pitch part. Power can have a destabilizing effect: an increase of power may tend to make the nose rise. Designers offset it with a high thrust line; a very low thrust line adds to the nose-up effect of the tail [[1:114|PHAK 5-17]]. In its instrument flying chapter, the AFH adds the same general point: a properly trimmed airplane takes a nose-up attitude on its own in proportion to the power applied, while torque and P-factor bank and turn it left [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

head: What adds to the pitch-up or yaw
What it does at the go-around
rows: Nose-up approach trim
Holds the elevator trailing edge up, set for a slow idle glide [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
More propwash over the tail
Adds to the trim and raises the nose sharply [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Thrust line
A low thrust line adds to the nose-up effect when power is added [[1:114|PHAK 5-17]]
Flaps beyond 15 degrees
A significant nose-up pitching moment in certain high-wing airplanes, because the downwash over the tail changes [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]
Spiraling slipstream
Very compact at high propeller speed and low forward speed, pushing the vertical tail and yawing the nose [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
P-factor
At high AOA the right (downswinging) blade bites more and yaws the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]

body.p: AC 61-67C calls a go-around, with its high pitch attitude, high power and low airspeed, a classic setting where P-factor can play a part in a stall/spin accident [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. The full left-turning story is in the Power-On Stalls lesson (AI.X.D). The pitch behavior with flaps depends on the design of the particular airplane [[24:233|AFH 12-2]], so check what yours does.

callout.text: Application: as the nose climbs, the speed bleeds off and the AOA grows. If the pilot does not push, the airplane flies itself toward the critical AOA with full power and a left yaw, which is the setup for a stall with a wing drop.

check.q: Why is the spiraling slipstream effect so strong right after full power is applied at approach speed?
check.a: The spiral is very compact at high propeller speed and low forward speed, so it exerts a strong sideward force on the vertical tail [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

chunks.title: Where it happens: the real go-around

body.p: The AFH lists three places this stall waits for a pilot, all with the trim set for a normal approach glide at idle power [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]:

bullets: A go-around from a normal landing approach.
A go-around from a simulated forced-landing approach.
Immediately after a takeoff (application: a touch-and-go where the approach trim was never reset).

body.p: The go-around itself rests on three principles, in order: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Full or maximum allowable takeoff power goes in smoothly and without hesitation; abrupt throttle movement can make some engines falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

When the pilot decides to go around, a trim setting for low airspeed is already in place. The sudden power raises the nose and causes left yaw; letting the nose rise too early could cause an unrecoverable stall when the go-around starts at low altitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The pilot should expect considerable forward elevator pressure to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude, use right rudder for torque and P-factor, and rough trim once the attitude and airspeed are right [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Attitude: an airplane cannot fly below stall speed, so resist any impulse to pitch up for a climb when the airspeed is too low; it may even be right to lower the nose briefly to gain speed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Close to the ground, ground effect lends performance that is repaid when the airplane climbs out of it; climbing too soon may leave the airplane unable to climb or hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

Task prioritization (R5): in airplanes with high control pressures at maximum power, use caution reaching for the flap handle; airplane control comes first in this high-workload phase [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Delays make it all worse. The AFH names landing expectancy and pride as the two usual sources of a late go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Application: make 'push and right rudder' part of the words of every go-around call in the pattern, so the hands and feet are already moving when the power comes in.

check.q: Your learner starts a go-around and immediately grabs the flap handle while the nose is climbing. What does the AFH say comes first?
check.a: Airplane control; use caution reaching for the flap handle when power produces high control pressures [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Hold the attitude with forward pressure first.

chunks.title: Recognizing it from the right seat

body.p: The cues that are special to this stall come first, before any stall warning: the nose rising sharply, the airplane turning left, and the pitch going above the normal climbing attitude after the throttle is fully advanced [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. In the real go-around, the pilot feels the need for considerable forward pressure to hold the nose [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Cue
What to point out to the learner
rows: Pitch attitude
Nose well above the normal climb picture, still rising [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Heading
Nose swinging left with the ball out of center [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
Feel
Control pressures change, and bigger control movements are needed as speed decays [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]
Sound
The air noise changes as the speed decreases [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]
Engine
In fixed-pitch airplanes, a loss of rpm may show near a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]
Stall warning
Many devices alert 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; buffet may begin just before [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]

body.p: Know which stall you are flying. An impending stall is when the AOA gives a stall warning but has not reached critical; a full stall is when the critical AOA is exceeded, usually shown by an uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot be readily stopped, sometimes with a roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The evaluator picks which one you show (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X).
ACS skill element S6: "Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)." Say them out loud: 'Nose high, turning left, horn. Recovering.'

callout.text: Application: learners connect stalls with pulling back. In this stall their hands may be light or even pushing a little while the trim and power raise the nose. Teach them to watch the attitude, not their own hands.

check.q: In a fixed-pitch trainer, which engine cue may show a power-on stall approaching as the nose climbs?

chunks.title: Setting it up: entry and minimum altitude

body.p: Brief first. CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task G: "The applicant and evaluator must brief the recovery prior to stall execution. A realistic scenario includes a simulated short-field approach at altitude trimmed for approach airspeed, low power, and full flaps." Use the same brief with every learner.
The AFH entry [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]:

head: ACS element
What you do
What you say
rows: S1 Clear the area
Clearing turns, looking at and below your altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
'Clear left, clear right, clear below.'
S2 Entry altitude
Pick an altitude to finish no lower than 3,000 ft AGL, plus a spin margin [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]
'Highest terrain is 1,800, so we finish above 4,800 and start near 5,800.'
S3 Throttle back, landing configuration
Slowly retard the throttle, gear down if retractable, flaps one-half or full, close the throttle, hold altitude as speed decays to normal glide speed [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
'Landing configuration, like short final.'
S4 Glide and trim
Establish the normal glide and trim nose-up for it [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
'Trimmed. My hands are light, the trim is holding the nose.'
S5 Go-around power
Advance the throttle smoothly to maximum allowable power, just as for a go-around [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
'Going around. Watch the nose.'

body.p: Minimum altitude. The CFI ACS asks you to "Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)." The AFH recommends stall practice that allows recovery no lower than 1,500 ft AGL in single-engine airplanes, or higher if the AFM/POH says so [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and AC 61-67C says the same for stall demonstrations [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]]. Teach the ACS figure for this Task. A full stall here needs a significant nose-down attitude and a significant loss of altitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and a spin's first turn loses about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].
For the short-field scenario, use the POH approach speed. When none is published, the AFH uses not more than 1.3 VSO, adding no more than half the gust factor in gusty air [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

AC 61-67C's version has the learner set the landing approach configuration in a trimmed descent, then go around with full power holding only light elevator and right rudder pressure, letting the nose pitch up and torque swerve the airplane left, and recovering at the first indication of a stall to a normal climbing pitch attitude [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200g]] [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

callout.text: S3: "Retard the throttle and configure the airplane for landing." S4: "Establish a normal glide airspeed and trim the airplane." S5: "Advance the throttle to the maximum allowable power as in a go-around."

check.q: What configuration and trim does the CFI ACS Appendix 3 call a realistic scenario for this Task?
check.a: A simulated short-field approach at altitude, trimmed for approach airspeed, with low power and full flaps (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task G); the AFH allows one-half or full flaps [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

body.p: The AFH recovery: when it is clear the airplane is approaching a stall, apply enough forward elevator pressure to reduce the AOA and eliminate the stall warning before returning to the normal climbing attitude. Then adjust the trim to relieve the heavy control pressures, complete the normal go-around procedure and return to the desired flightpath [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. From a full stall the recovery needs a significant nose-down attitude and a significant loss of altitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

head: Step
Hands and feet
Why
rows: 1. Reduce AOA
Forward pressure until the warning stops
AOA first, every time [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
2. Stop the yaw, wings level
Right rudder, then ailerons
Cancel yaw so the stall does not become a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
3. Power
Confirm it is still at maximum allowable
Already set, so this may simply mean confirming it [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
4. Climb attitude
Ease to the normal climb picture
Avoid a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]
5. Retrim
Nose-down trim to take off the push
Relieve the heavy pressures [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
6. Clean up
Flaps up in small increments as speed builds, then gear if retractable
A sudden full retraction can cost lift [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

body.p: Where trim fits in the template. Step 2b says to trim nose-down if the elevator does not give the needed response, but excessive trim may aggravate the condition or cause loss of control or high structural loads [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. In a training airplane, trim is less of a concern because most pilots can overpower it, and improper trim can be corrected while returning to the desired flightpath [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. So: push first, trim second.

Recovery risks (R1). Too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by putting a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Rushing back to a climb before flying speed returns causes a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. Application: the trim is still nose-up after the stall warning stops, so if the learner relaxes the push before retrimming, the nose comes straight back up.

callout.text: S7: "Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator." S8: "Adjust trim and return to the desired flightpath." AC 61-67C asks you to stress correct attitude control, control pressures and proper trim during go-arounds [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

check.q: The stall warning has stopped, the airplane is in a normal climb, and your learner's arms are shaking from holding the yoke forward. What does the AFH have them do next?
check.a: Adjust the trim to relieve the heavy control pressures, then complete the normal go-around and return to the desired flightpath [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

chunks.title: Aircraft limitations and the spin risk

body.p: This demonstration combines full flaps, full power and, in the recovery, a nose-down attitude. That is a fast way to meet the airplane's limits. Know them from the POH before you fly it.

bullets: Flap speed: VFE is the top of the white arc, the maximum speed with flaps extended [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]], set by the air loads on the flaps [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. For light-sport airplanes the AFH warns that VFE comes quickly if full power and a nose-down attitude are held [[24:347|AFH 17-13]]. Application: the same watch applies in any trainer after a full trim stall.
Red lines: never let the airspeed indicator or the tachometer reach its red line during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

G with flaps out: accelerated stalls are never practiced with flaps extended because of the lower design G-load limits in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Application: the pull-out after a full trim stall must be smooth, since load factor builds in the pull-up [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].
Power: use maximum allowable power from the POH, applied smoothly; abrupt throttle can make some engines falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

CG: with an aft CG, less elevator force is needed to stall and inadvertent stalls come easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]. Application: an aft load adds to the pitch-up you are about to show.

body.p: The spin. A spin needs a stall plus sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall, and engine and propeller effects (P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream) are among the causes of yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. This stall comes with full power and a left yaw already in place. In airplanes placarded against spins there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. If a spin does start, the first step for an upright spin is to close the throttle completely [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]], which matters here because the throttle is wide open.

callout.text: Application: recover at the first sign of a wing drop or yaw that the rudder is not stopping. A trim stall demonstration that turns into rotation is no longer a demonstration.

check.q: You are recovering from a full trim stall with full flaps, full power and the nose well down. Which airspeed limit is closest, and what does AC 61-67C say about red lines?
check.a: VFE, the top of the white arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]; the airspeed indicator and tachometer should never reach their red lines during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

chunks.title: Environment: turbulence, microbursts and density altitude

body.p: The ACS wording for R2 in this Task reads: "Effect of environmental elements on airplane performance related to cross-controlled stalls (e.g., turbulence, microbursts, and high-density altitude)." It appears to be carried over from Task F. Teach the same elements as they affect a go-around with approach trim.

head: Element
What the sources say
What it means for a trim stall (application)
rows: Turbulence

A vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA, and the stall may come while the pilot is fighting to control the flightpath, especially on a gusty approach; fly a higher approach speed in moderate or severe turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]
A gust during the pitch-up adds AOA on top of the trim and power. Keep the nose lower and push sooner.
Microbursts

Downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots; a typical microburst is 1 to 2 miles across and lasts 5 to 15 minutes; on approach it can force the airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]
The first headwind raises the speed and the nose-up trim lifts the nose more. When the tailwind arrives the airplane is nose high and slowing.
High density altitude

Little or no effect on indicated stall speed, but performance decreases and true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]; less dense air decreases engine power output [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]]; spin altitude losses are greater [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]
Less power means a weaker climb. A learner may hold the nose high 'to make it climb', which is the stall setup.

callout.text: Application: on gusty or hot days, add one line to the go-around brief: 'Pitch for airspeed, not for climb rate.' It ties straight back to the AFH warning not to pitch up when the airspeed is insufficient [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: On a hot, high afternoon, what stays the same and what gets worse for a go-around with approach trim?
check.a: The indicated stall speed stays about the same, but performance decreases, true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]] and the engine makes less power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

body.p: Collision hazards (R3). Clearing turns make sure the next maneuver will not fly into another aircraft's path; teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on it before every training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. The AIM lists stalls among the maneuvers that need clearing first [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Training airspace is often crowded and hazy [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and if learners think the instructor does all the scanning they never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Application, specific to this stall: the nose climbs well above the climb attitude and swings left, so the forward and left view is blocked and the heading changes. Clear in the direction the airplane will swing, and look again after the recovery.

Distractions and task prioritization (R5). The AIH names preoccupation inside or outside the flight deck while changing aircraft configuration or trim as a setup for a stall/spin [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. A go-around is exactly that moment: power, trim, flaps, radio, traffic. AC 61-67C adds that stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with other tasks [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. Losing situational awareness and failing to return to the desired flightpath is on the AFH error list [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Disorientation (R5). After a turn long enough for the inner-ear fluid to move with the canal, a head movement in a different plane, such as looking down at the trim wheel or flap lever, can cause the coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. A rapid acceleration, as with full power, can give the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude in poor visual conditions, and the pilot may push into a nose-low attitude [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Application: at night or in haze, hold the attitude by reference to the attitude indicator, and trim by feel without looking down.

callout.text: Go-around order: Power, Attitude, Configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Trim lives inside Attitude: push, rudder, then rough trim.

check.q: When can looking down at the trim wheel or flap lever set off the coriolis illusion?
check.a: After a turn long enough for the inner-ear fluid to move with the canal; a head movement in a different plane can then start the fluid moving [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Keep the head up and trim by feel.

body.p: Ground first. Stalls are learned better when the types and their aerodynamics are discussed on the ground, and the task should be reviewed before the flight even if it was covered in ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. For this stall, draw the tail, the trim tab and the propwash on the whiteboard and show where the forces come from.
Build it in blocks, from known to unknown [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]:

head: Block
What the learner sees
Source
rows: 1. Trim at slow speed
In slow flight, the effect of elevator trim at neutral and at full nose-up, plus the left-turning tendency and right rudder
2. Power-on stalls
Recognition and recovery at high power (lesson AI.X.D)
3. Elevator trim stall demonstration
At altitude, your demonstration with narration, then the learner's
4. Go-arounds in the pattern
Push, right rudder, rough trim, flaps in steps
5. Variations
Go-around from a simulated forced landing approach and from a low go-around near the ground

body.p: Narrate the demonstration. Explain the power settings and attitudes as you fly, and fly it exactly the way you want the learner to practice it, because learners imitate the instructor [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A sample (application): 'Glide trimmed, hands light. Full power, smoothly. I am holding only light pressure. See the nose climb past our climb picture? Swinging left. Horn. Push, right rudder, horn is off. Climb attitude. Now I trim nose-down to take off this heavy push. Flaps up a notch at a time.'

Then let the learner talk you through it while you fly; it lets you check their understanding before they are busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. AC 61-67C's plan has the learner fly it too [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200g]]; whether and when is your judgment and syllabus. Close with AC 61-67C's three emphasis points: correct attitude control, application of control pressures, and proper trim during go-arounds [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

callout.text: Application: for S9, finish with the three real-world settings the AFH lists (go-around from a normal approach, from a simulated forced landing, and right after takeoff with approach trim) [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and ask the learner what each has in common.

check.q: In AC 61-67C's stall avoidance practice at slow airspeed, which two elevator trim settings does the instructor demonstrate?

body.p: This stall surprises learners because they did not cause it with their hands. An anxious learner reacting to stalls may go into a fight-or-flight response, with little time to think [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Before stalls, review the aerodynamics, then describe the sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Here: 'The nose will come up hard and swing left. It is the airplane, not you. We push and add right rudder.'

bullets: Brief the exchange of flight controls before the flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. During your demonstration the learner follows lightly; you are flying.
When the learner flies it, be alert and ready to take control, especially on the first attempt [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Guard the controls. If needed, take control and calmly say 'I have the flight controls'; anxious learners can be very strong, and nothing is gained by fighting them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Watch the trim hand. Application: a startled learner may spin the trim wheel instead of pushing. The template warns that excessive trim can aggravate the situation or cause loss of control [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Allow enough time and space to take over before the situation deteriorates beyond your ability [[25:190|AIH 10-6]], and never exceed your own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Know the airplane: familiarize yourself with the model and its POH before instructing in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

callout.text: Application: agree a take-over point in the brief, for example 'if the horn sounds and I do not feel you pushing, I will take it.' Then do it.

check.q: Your learner flies the trim stall, hands light, and freezes as the nose climbs and the horn sounds. What do you do?
check.a: Take control and calmly say 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], then push to eliminate the warning, right rudder, climb attitude and retrim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

body.p: On the checkride the evaluator may fly as your learner and make these errors; you analyze and correct them (S10: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task."). Built from the AFH stall error list [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], the go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] and the trim stall text [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]:

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear the area
Configuring without looking, or not looking left before the swing
Clear at and below, and toward the swing [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Abrupt power application
Throttle slammed in; engine may falter
Smooth, positive power [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Not anticipating the pitch-up (improper pitch attitude)
Light hands, nose well above the climb picture
Expect considerable forward pressure and hold the attitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Failure to compensate for torque/P-factor
Nose swings left, ball out
Right rudder as the power comes in [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Inability to recognize an impending stall
Horn sounds and nothing happens
Name the cues out loud; recover at the first one [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Not keeping the push until the warning stops
Push, then relax with the horn still on
Nose-down input until the warning is gone [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Excessive forward-elevator pressure
Low or negative G, items float
Only enough push to stop the warning [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]
Trimming instead of pushing
Learner spins the wheel, nose still high
Push first; trim after; excessive trim can aggravate it [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
No retrim after recovery
Nose creeps back up, second warning
Rough trim nose-down, then fine-trim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Inadvertent secondary stall
Second buffet as the nose comes up
Let flying speed return first [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]
Sudden, complete flap retraction
Airplane settles as the lever goes to up
Flaps up in small increments as speed builds [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Excessive airspeed buildup
Steep dive after a full stall; speed toward the white arc top
Start a smooth pull as soon as the warning is gone; watch VFE [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Losing situational awareness
Heading and altitude wander after the recovery
Return to the desired flightpath [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]

body.p: Find the root cause, not only the symptom. When the learner talks through the go-around, you can tell a misconception ('the trim will sort itself out') from a lack of motor skill (says 'push', but the arms do not) [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: safety permitting, let the learner go a little way into the pitch-up at altitude and find the push themselves; learners seldom learn a maneuver well without the chance to correct an error [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Never in the pattern.

check.q: After the recovery your learner moves the flap lever straight to up in one motion and the airplane sinks. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Sudden, complete flap retraction, which can cause a loss of lift; retract them in small increments as the airplane accelerates [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-14. Elevator trim stall. (AFH 5-21)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane flies a curving path in four stages under the title Elevator Trim Stall: configure for landing, establish normal glide speed while straight-and-level, then trim nose-up; apply maximum allowable power to simulate a go-around and allow the nose to rise; prior to a full stall, apply forward pressure, eliminate the stall warning, establish a normal climb attitude and re-trim; return to the desired flightpath.

f2.caption: Figure 6-20. The movement of the elevator is opposite to the direction of movement of the elevator trim tab. (PHAK 6-11)
f2.alt: Two side views of a tail with airflow lines. Top panel, Nose-down trim: the trim tab is deflected up and the elevator down, labeled Tab up, elevator down. Bottom panel, Nose-up trim: the elevator is deflected up and the trim tab is bent down relative to it; the printed label under this panel still reads Tab up, elevator up.

f3.caption: Figure 5-24. Effect of speed on downwash. (PHAK 5-16)
f3.alt: Three airplanes with dotted downwash lines flowing back to the tail and a tail-load arrow beside each. Cruise speed: balanced tail load. Low speed: downwash angled away, lesser downward tail load. High speed: greater downward tail load.

f4.caption: Figure 5-27. Power changes affect longitudinal stability. (PHAK 5-17)
f4.alt: Three airplanes with lift, thrust and CG marked. Cruise power: level. Idle power: a purple arrow shows the nose pitching down, with a faded copy of the airplane nose low. Full power: a purple arrow shows the nose pitching up, with a faded copy of the airplane nose high.

f5.caption: Figure 5-48. Corkscrewing slipstream. (PHAK 5-31)
f5.alt: An airplane drawn at an angle from the front left. An orange spiral labeled Slipstream wraps around the fuselage from the propeller and reaches the tail, labeled Force where it pushes on the vertical tail, with curved blue arrows labeled Yaw at the nose and at the tail.

f6.caption: Figure 9-12. Go-around procedure. (AFH 9-11)
f6.alt: An airplane over a runway in stages: timely decision to make go-around; apply max power, adjust pitch attitude and allow airspeed to increase; assume climb attitude, flaps to intermediate; positive rate of climb, retract gear, climb at VY; retract remaining flaps; 500 feet cruise climb.

f7.caption: Figure 5-10. Stall recovery template. (AFH 5-15)
f7.alt: A table titled Stall Recovery Template: 1 wing leveler or autopilot, disconnect; 2a pitch nose-down, apply until impending stall indications are eliminated; 2b trim nose-down pitch, as needed; 3 bank, wings level; 4 thrust or power, as needed; 5 speed brakes or spoilers, retract; 6 return to the desired flight path.

scenario.title: A go-around that got away, and tomorrow's demonstration
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Today, on short final with full flaps and the trim set for the approach, your pre-solo learner was told to go around. They pushed the throttle in all at once with light hands; the nose pitched up steeply, the airplane yawed left and the stall horn sounded before you pushed the nose down. Tomorrow you plan an elevator trim stall demonstration in the same fixed-pitch, high-wing trainer, which is placarded against intentional spins. The practice area is in Class E airspace with terrain up to 1,200 ft MSL, the forecast is broken clouds at 5,500 ft MSL, wind 15 gusting 25 knots, and a hot afternoon.

questions.q: What happened on today's go-around, in the AFH's terms?
questions.a: The trim was set for low airspeed, so the sudden power raised the nose and caused left yaw; the learner did not apply the considerable forward pressure and right rudder needed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. That is the elevator trim stall setup: propwash plus nose-up trim making the nose rise sharply and turn left [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Abrupt power is also a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: What is the lowest altitude at which the Task may be completed, and does the cloud layer leave room for a spin margin?
questions.a: 1,200 + 3,000 = 4,200 ft MSL (AI.X.G.S2). Adding about 1,000 ft for a first spin turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] gives 5,200 ft MSL, but in Class E below 10,000 ft MSL you must stay 500 ft below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]], so 5,000 ft MSL is the highest you can be under a 5,500 ft base. That leaves only 800 ft above the floor, and the pitch-up itself climbs toward the clouds (application). Do not teach stalls below a cloud layer that does not allow enough altitude to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application: find another area or another day, or teach a different lesson.

questions.q: How do the gusts change the demonstration and the next pattern lesson?
questions.a: A vertical gust can suddenly raise the AOA, and the stall may come while the pilot is fighting to hold the flightpath; use a higher approach speed in strong, gusty conditions [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. With no POH figure, the AFH short-field speed is not more than 1.3 VSO plus no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

questions.q: The trainer is placarded against spins. What does that mean for how far you take the stall?
questions.a: There is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Recover at the first sign of a wing drop or uncontrolled yaw; if rotation starts, close the throttle first [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Brief the recovery and your take-over point on the ground, just as the CFI ACS requires you and the evaluator to brief the recovery before the stall (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task G).

questions.q: What will you look for during clearing, given what the airplane does in this stall?
questions.a: Clear the area at and below before the maneuver [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Application: the nose will rise well above the climb attitude and swing left, so look hard to the left and ahead, and clear again after recovery. Hazy, crowded training areas raise the collision risk [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: After the demonstration, how do you describe to the learner the conditions that lead to this stall, for future avoidance (S9)?
questions.a: A go-around from a normal approach, a go-around from a simulated forced-landing approach, or a takeoff right after landing, each with the trim set for the idle approach glide [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Then stress correct attitude control, control pressures and proper trim during go-arounds [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

skills.do: "Clear the area." Clearing turns, with spoken callouts, looking at and below your altitude and toward the left swing.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns before every stall with the same words you want learners to copy [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: "Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)." Say the terrain height, the floor and your spin margin.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write the practice area's highest terrain, add 3,000 ft and a spin margin of about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], and check it against the cloud base.

skills.do: "Retard the throttle and configure the airplane for landing." Slowly reduce power, gear down if retractable, flaps one-half or full, throttle closed, altitude held.
skills.practice: Run the flow aloud on the ground with the POH open: flap limits, VFE and approach speeds [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: "Establish a normal glide airspeed and trim the airplane." Show the learner the trim is now holding the nose.
skills.practice: Practice stabilizing at the POH approach speed and trimming until the pressure is gone [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

skills.do: "Advance the throttle to the maximum allowable power as in a go-around." Smoothly, holding only light pressure while you narrate the pitch-up and left turn.
skills.practice: With another instructor, fly the entry until the throttle movement is smooth and your narration matches what the airplane does [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: "Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)." Call them out loud.
skills.practice: On every power-on stall and go-around, call 'nose high, turning left, horn' as each cue appears [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

skills.do: "Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator." Forward pressure until the warning stops, right rudder, climb attitude.
skills.practice: Brief both versions with the evaluator first (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Task G), and practice the full stall version only with ample altitude, noting the altitude lost [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: "Adjust trim and return to the desired flightpath." Rough trim nose-down, flaps up in increments, then fine-trim on course and altitude.
skills.practice: Fly pattern go-arounds at altitude: push, rudder, rough trim, flaps in steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: "Describe and demonstrate conditions that lead to an elevator trim stall for future avoidance." Name the three settings and fly the demonstration while explaining it.
skills.practice: Write a narration script and say it in a chair-flying session until it fits the airplane's timing [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task." Watch the evaluator-learner, name the error and give the fix.
skills.practice: Have another instructor fly the common errors at altitude while you name and correct each one [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

quiz.q: With the trim wheel set full nose-up in a typical small airplane, what are the trim tab and elevator doing?
options: Tab deflected up, airflow holding the elevator trailing edge up
Tab deflected down, airflow holding the elevator trailing edge up
Tab deflected down, airflow holding the elevator trailing edge down
Tab and elevator both faired, with the stabilizer angle doing the work
quiz.why: Full nose-up moves the tab full down, and the air under the tail forces the elevator trailing edge up [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

quiz.q: Why does closing the throttle make a trimmed airplane's nose drop, according to the PHAK?
options: Propeller drag at idle pulls the nose down below the thrust line
Less downwash reaches the tail, so the tail-down force drops
Torque reaction at idle rolls and pitches the nose downward
The CG moves forward as fuel flow to the engine decreases
quiz.why: Closing the throttle reduces the wing's downwash, and the force on the stabilizer is no longer enough to hold the tail down [[1:114|PHAK 5-17]].

quiz.q: Which thrust line arrangement does the PHAK say adds to the nose-up effect of the tail when power is added?
options: A high thrust line passing well above the CG
A thrust line passing exactly through the CG
A thrust line angled slightly to the right
A very low thrust line
quiz.why: A high thrust line counters the nose rise; a very low thrust line adds to the nose-up effect of the horizontal tail [[1:114|PHAK 5-17]].

quiz.q: In certain high-wing airplanes, what does flap deflection beyond 15 degrees produce, according to the AFH?
options: Mostly lift with little drag and a nose-down moment
A strong left yaw from the flap on the propeller side
A significant nose-up pitching moment from the change in downwash over the tail
No pitch change, because the flap moment and the downwash cancel
quiz.why: Beyond 15 degrees, flaps add a large increase in drag and a significant nose-up pitching moment in certain high-wing airplanes because the downwash changes the airflow over the tail [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

quiz.q: The AFH names two usual sources of delay in starting a go-around. Which pair is it?
options: Landing expectancy and pride
Fatigue and a heavy workload
Fixation on airspeed and tower instructions
Ground effect and a gusty crosswind
quiz.why: Delay normally stems from landing expectancy (set) and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: In the AFH stall recovery template, when may nose-down pitch trim be needed?
options: Always, right after the wing leveler is disconnected
Only after the wings are level and power is set
Never in a single-engine airplane without autopilot
If the elevator alone does not give the needed response
quiz.why: Step 2b: trim nose-down if the elevator does not provide the needed response; excessive trim may aggravate the condition [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: What is the lowest altitude at which the CFI ACS lets you complete the elevator trim stall Task?
options: 1,500 ft AGL, the AFH stall practice figure
3,000 ft AGL
2,000 ft AGL, plus a margin for spin recovery
3,000 ft MSL or the POH figure, whichever is higher
quiz.why: AI.X.G.S2: completed "no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)". The AFH general figure is 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: During a go-around, when does the AFH have the pilot 'rough trim' the airplane?
options: As the throttle reaches full power, before the attitude is set
Before the power comes in, while still on the approach glide
Only after the flaps and gear are fully retracted at altitude
After the right airspeed and the climb attitude are set
quiz.why: After attaining the appropriate airspeed and adjusting pitch attitude for a climb, the pilot rough trims to relieve adverse control pressures; finer trim comes once conditions stabilize [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: The AIH lists preoccupations that can create a stall/spin situation. Which one fits a go-around best?
options: Reading a long checklist during cruise flight
Tuning the radios while taxiing out
Changing aircraft configuration or trim
Filing a flight plan by phone before departure
quiz.why: Preoccupation while changing aircraft configuration or trim, maneuvering to avoid traffic or clearing obstacles can create a potential stall/spin situation [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: For a stall in a fixed-pitch propeller airplane at high power, which engine cue does AC 61-67C mention?
options: A rise in oil temperature
A sudden drop in fuel flow
A loss of rpm
A rise in manifold pressure
quiz.why: In fixed-pitch propeller airplanes, a loss of rpm may be evident when approaching a stall in power-on conditions [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks why the left swing in this demonstration matters so much. Which setting does AC 61-67C call a classic one for P-factor in a stall/spin accident?
options: A go-around: high pitch attitude, high power and low airspeed
A slow cruise descent at low power with the flaps up and trim set
A steep turn at maneuvering speed with the ball centered throughout
A power-off glide at best glide speed with full nose-up trim set
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C names a go-around or short-field takeoff, with a high pitch attitude, high power setting and low airspeed, as a classic situation where P-factor could play an important role in a stall/spin accident [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

final_quiz.q: During your full stall demonstration the left wing drops hard and the airplane starts to rotate with full power on. Per AC 61-67C, what is the first step of an upright spin recovery?
options: Full right aileron to raise the low wing
Close the throttle completely
Hold full power to keep the airflow over the tail
Full forward elevator, then rudder
final_quiz.why: The first step in recovering from an upright spin is to close the throttle completely [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]; in placarded airplanes there is no assurance of recovery from a developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: After a good recovery, your learner relaxes the forward pressure to rest their arms, and the nose climbs again with a second horn. What is happening and what is the fix?
options: The approach trim is still in; hold the push and retrim nose-down
The flaps are still out; raise them all at once to drop the nose
Ground effect has ended; add more power to keep it climbing
P-factor is raising the nose; add left rudder to stop it
final_quiz.why: The pilot must adjust the trim to relieve the heavy control pressures before completing the go-around [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; raising the nose before flying speed returns risks a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

final_quiz.q: On a touch-and-go, your learner leaves the trim where it was for the approach and adds full power. Which elevator trim stall setting from the AFH is this?
options: A go-around from a simulated forced-landing approach
A balked landing flown in ground effect after a bounce on the touchdown
Immediately after takeoff, with the trim set for the approach glide
A departure stall entered from a climbing turn after takeoff
final_quiz.why: The AFH lists this stall during a go-around or immediately after a takeoff, with the trim set for a normal landing approach glide at idle power [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Recovering from a full trim stall, your learner holds full power with the nose well down and full flaps. The airspeed is nearing the top of the white arc. What is the concern?
options: VFE, set by air loads on the extended flaps
The power-on stall speed rising with the airspeed
Gyroscopic precession pitching the nose further down
The lower limit of the green arc being exceeded
final_quiz.why: The top of the white arc is VFE, the maximum speed with flaps extended [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]], because of the air loads on the flaps [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. Never let red lines be reached in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

final_quiz.q: Before your demonstration, your learner loads two heavy bags in the aft baggage area, still within limits. Per AC 61-67C, what does the aft CG change?
options: More elevator force is needed to stall, so the trim stall is milder
Nothing that matters, as long as the CG is inside the approved envelope
Less elevator force reaches a high AOA, so inadvertent stalls come easier
The stall speed rises sharply, so the horn sounds well before the pitch-up
final_quiz.why: As the CG moves aft, less elevator deflection and control force are needed to reach a high AOA, which can make inadvertent stalls easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]]; it is a forward CG that needs more back force [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]].

final_quiz.q: At the first stall cue, your learner reaches for the trim wheel and runs in a lot of nose-down trim before pushing. What do you tell them?
options: That is the AFH technique; trim is the first step for pitch
Push first; excessive trim can aggravate it or overload the airplane
Trim works faster than elevator at low airspeeds
It is fine as long as the trim is reset to takeoff afterward
final_quiz.why: The template uses trim only if the elevator does not give the needed response, and excessive trim may aggravate the condition, cause loss of control or high structural loads [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]; in a trainer most pilots can overpower the trim [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: In the simulated approach glide, your learner holds steady back pressure on the yoke to keep the glide speed. What does the PHAK say that pressure tells you?
options: Nose-up trim is needed; keep trimming until the pressure is gone
The trim is set correctly, since some back pressure is normal in a glide
Nose-down trim is needed, because the tab is already too far down
The elevator is near its stop, so the power should be increased instead
final_quiz.why: Constant back pressure on the control column indicates the need for nose-up trim; keep trimming until the nose-heavy condition is gone [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]. That is the trim the go-around power then acts on [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: On a gusty day, during the pitch-up of your demonstration, a sharp bump hits and the horn sounds early. What does AC 61-67C say about this?
options: Gusts lower the stall speed, so the horn is a false alarm
A vertical gust can suddenly raise the AOA and stall the airplane
Turbulence only matters above maneuvering speed
Gusts affect power-off stalls but not power-on stalls
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust or wind shear can cause an abrupt increase in AOA, and the stall may occur while the pilot is controlling the flightpath [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

final_quiz.q: You will demonstrate the full trim stall from a high practice area on a hot afternoon. Which planning point does AC 61-67C support?
options: Fly a lower indicated approach speed, since the true airspeed is higher
Expect the stall at a clearly higher indicated airspeed than at sea level
Use a lower entry altitude, since thin air shortens any recovery dive
Allow more altitude margin; spins lose more height at high density altitude
final_quiz.why: Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed, and the recommended indicated speeds should be kept [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]; greater spin altitude losses can be expected at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

final_quiz.q: Debriefing a go-around stall/spin accident report with a learner, which causal factor in such accidents does AC 61-67C name?
options: Retracting the landing gear before a positive rate of climb was shown
Flying the approach too fast, which caused a long float and a late decision
Using carburetor heat during the go-around, which cut the available power
Losing positive control due to nose-high trim or early flap retraction
final_quiz.why: Many power-on stall/spin accidents occurred during go-arounds; a causal factor was the pilot's failure to maintain positive control due to a nose-high trim setting or premature flap retraction [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]].

final_quiz.q: You move to a low-wing trainer for this demonstration. Your learner says, 'Flaps always pitch the nose up, so the pitch-up will be the same.' What does the AFH say?
options: It depends on the design: nose-up, nose-down or almost no change
Wrong; flaps only ever pitch the nose down in low-wing airplanes
Correct; flap extension adds a nose-up moment in every design
Flap effects vanish at full power, so only the trim setting matters
final_quiz.why: As flaps are deflected, the airplane may pitch nose-up, nose-down or have minimal change; the pitch behavior depends on the design of the particular airplane [[24:233|AFH 12-2]]. Fly it with another instructor in each new model.

final_quiz.q: Which three emphasis points does AC 61-67C give for closing the elevator trim stall demonstration?
options: Clearing turns, radio calls to the tower and the use of the go-around checklist
Stall speed, maximum flap extended speed and the design maneuvering speed
Correct attitude control, control pressures and proper trim during go-arounds
Right rudder, carburetor heat and mixture
final_quiz.why: Emphasize the importance of correct attitude control, application of control pressures, and proper trim during go-arounds [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]].

takeaways: On final the trim is far nose-up, because a slow, power-off glide needs it.
Full power adds propwash over the tail: the nose rises sharply and swings left by itself.
It happens on go-arounds and right after a touch-and-go with approach trim still set.
Expect considerable forward pressure and right rudder the moment the power comes in.
Recover: push until the warning stops, rudder, climb attitude, then retrim and raise flaps in steps.
Set up at altitude to finish no lower than 3,000 ft AGL, and brief the recovery first.
Push first, trim second: excessive trim can make it worse.
cfi_notes: R2 in this Task says 'related to cross-controlled stalls', apparently copied from Task F. Teach turbulence, microbursts and density altitude as they affect a go-around with approach trim, and mention the wording if the evaluator asks.

Altitude: the AFH recommends stall practice with recovery no lower than 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] and AC 61-67C says the same [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]], but the CFI ACS asks for completion no lower than 3,000 ft AGL (AI.X.G.S2). Fly and teach the ACS figure for this Task, plus a spin margin.

Flaps: the AFH says one-half or full [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], the ACS Appendix 3 scenario says full flaps, and AC 61-67C says landing approach configuration [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200g]]. Use full flaps when the POH allows it and brief it.

Recovery order: AC 61-67C says recover at the first indication to a normal climbing pitch attitude [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200g]] [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]]; the AFH says first eliminate the stall warning with forward pressure, then return to the climb attitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Teach the AFH order.

Who flies it: the AFH calls it demonstration-only for certification [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], while AC 61-67C's plan has the student fly it [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200g]]. Decide by syllabus and learner readiness, and be ready to take control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

PHAK Figure 6-20's printed label under the nose-up panel reads 'Tab up, elevator up', but the drawing above it shows the tab bent down against an up elevator, and the PHAK text says nose-up trim moves the tab to its full down position [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] and that elevator trim tabs move opposite to the elevator [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]. The label is a misprint: teach 'tab down, elevator up' and point it out if a learner asks.

Trim forces vary: the AFH says most pilots can overpower the trim in a training airplane [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], but warns that some airplanes produce high control pressures at maximum power on go-arounds [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Show the demonstration in each new make and model with another instructor first.
In the AIH midair study, flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. The pitch-up and left swing of this stall block your view; clear toward the swing.
gaps: No source gives how high the nose will go, how fast, or the push force needed in a given trainer. Fly it with another instructor and note the numbers for your airplane.
The altitude lost in a full elevator trim stall is given only as 'significant' [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; measure it at altitude in your airplane.
Whether a particular airplane tends to drop a wing or spin from a full-power stall, and its spin approval, come from the POH/AFM and placards, not the handbooks.
The value of 'maximum allowable power' and any engine limits for the demonstration come from the POH.
No source gives a narration script or the exact take-over point for a learner flying it. Write your own and use it every time.

activities.title: True or false: trim and power
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A zero reading on the trim indicator always means neutral trim.
cards.why: False. Downwash from the wing and fuselage on the tail means zero is not necessarily neutral trim [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

cards.s: Pilots normally set power, pitch attitude and configuration first, then trim off the pressure.
cards.why: True. That is the normal trim procedure, and any change of power, attitude or configuration needs a retrim [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]].

cards.s: Because nobody is pulling back, an elevator trim stall cannot exceed the critical AOA.
cards.why: False. The critical AOA can be exceeded at any airspeed, attitude and power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

cards.s: A certificated airplane's trim must be able to hold it in a normal power-off glide.
cards.why: True. The trimming device must be capable of holding the airplane in a normal glide with the power off [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

cards.s: The spiraling slipstream's rolling moment is to the right, partly opposing torque reaction.
cards.why: True. The corkscrew flow rolls the airplane right while torque reaction acts left; one may partly counteract the other [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

cards.s: The AFH says most pilots cannot overpower the trim in a training airplane, so trim must come first.
cards.why: False. Most pilots can overpower the trim in these airplanes; reduce AOA first and correct the trim later [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

activities.title: Numbers for the brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The highest terrain in your practice area is 2,100 ft MSL. What is the lowest MSL altitude at which the CFI ACS lets you complete this Task?
You add a margin above that floor equal to the altitude the AFH says the first turn of a spin costs. At what altitude do you start the setup?
items.why: The first spin turn loses about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]: 5,100 + 1,000 = 6,100 ft MSL.

items.q: From that 6,100 ft entry, a spin goes two full turns before recovery. Using the AFH figures (about 1,000 ft for the first turn, half that for each later turn), where are you?
items.why: 1,000 + 500 = 1,500 ft; 6,100 - 1,500 = 4,600 ft MSL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], 500 ft below the 5,100 ft floor. The margin covers one turn only: recover before rotation.

items.q: Your trainer's VSO is 47 knots and the POH gives no short-field approach speed. Using the AFH limit, what is the highest approach speed for the simulated short-field approach in calm air?
Same airplane, wind 12 gusting 22 knots. Adding the most the AFH allows for gusts, what approach speed do you brief?
items.why: Gust factor 22 - 12 = 10 knots; half is 5; 61.1 + 5 = 66.1, about 66 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator plays your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant. The evaluator acts as a private pilot learner seeing the elevator trim stall for the first time. Highest terrain in the practice area is 900 ft MSL. The recovery was briefed on the ground.

steps.s: Level at 3,700 ft MSL, the 'learner' reaches for the throttle to start the setup. What do you say?
options: Go ahead, but only show the impending version from here
Stop: we climb so we finish no lower than 3,900 ft MSL, with a spin margin above that
Go ahead; 3,700 ft is above the 1,500 ft AGL stall figure
Stop: descend to 3,000 ft AGL exactly so the picture is realistic
steps.why: 900 + 3,000 = 3,900 ft MSL floor (AI.X.G.S2), and the first spin turn loses about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

steps.s: Configured and trimmed in the glide, the 'learner' says they will add full power with both hands off the yoke 'to see what the trim does'. Your reply?
options: Fine; it shows the trim effect best
Hands on, and hold full forward pressure before adding power
Hands on: hold light elevator and right rudder pressure as the power comes in
Fine, but add the power slowly over ten seconds
steps.why: AC 61-67C has the go-around flown holding only light elevator and right rudder pressure [[13:18|AC 61-67C 200g]]; positive control is the point of the demonstration [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: The nose is well above the climb attitude, swinging left, horn on. The 'learner' starts cranking nose-down trim with the nose still high. What do you correct?
options: Nothing; trim is the strongest pitch control
Push the yoke forward until the warning stops; trim comes after
Pull the power to idle to stop the pitch-up
Level the wings with aileron first, then trim
steps.why: Reduce AOA with forward pressure until the warning stops [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; excessive trim may aggravate the condition [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: Warning gone, climb attitude set, the 'learner' moves the flap lever straight to up. What do you say?
options: Flaps up in small increments as the airplane accelerates
Put the flaps back to full for the rest of the climb
Good; less drag means a faster climb
Retract the gear first, then the flaps
steps.why: Retract flaps in small increments; a sudden complete retraction can cause a loss of lift [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

steps.s: Back at cruise, the evaluator asks where this stall could happen in real flying (S9). Which answer is complete?
options: Steep turns and accelerated maneuvers above VA
A skidding base-to-final turn with crossed controls
Slow flight with the stall horn on
Go-arounds from a normal or simulated forced-landing approach, and just after takeoff, with approach trim set
steps.why: The AFH lists a go-around from a normal or simulated forced-landing approach, or immediately after takeoff, with the trim set for the approach glide [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
